books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Treaty of December 30, 1853 (Gadsden Purchase), Article I, as ratified; Article III as ratified set the payment at $10 million. Public domain.
stimulus.text:
Article I. The Mexican Republic agrees to designate the following as her true limits with the United States for the future: . . . Beginning in the Gulf of Mexico, three leagues from land, opposite the mouth of the Rio Grande, as provided in the 5th article of the treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo; thence, as defined in the said article, up the middle of that river to the point where the parallel of 31° 47′ north latitude crosses the same; thence due west one hundred miles; thence south to the parallel of 31° 20′ north latitude; thence along the said parallel of 31° 20′ to the 111th meridian of longitude west of Greenwich; thence in a straight line to a point on the Colorado River twenty English miles below the junction of the Gila and Colorado rivers . . .

[Article III, as ratified, set the payment to Mexico at $10 million.]

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The Gadsden Treaty also released the United States from its 1848 promise, in Article XI of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, to stop Indian raids from American territory into Mexico. That release best shows which of the following?

options.text: That Mexico had stopped all Indian raids into the United States by 1853.
options.misconception: Raids continued on both sides of the border; the release was about the American promise, not Mexican raids.

options.text: That the United States had fulfilled its 1848 promise completely.
options.misconception: The United States could not keep the promise — the raids continued — which is why it sought release from it.

options.text: That the 1848 treaty had never mentioned Indian peoples at all.
options.misconception: Article XI of the 1848 treaty dealt directly with Indian incursions into Mexico.

options.text: That an unkeepable treaty promise became a bargaining chip in the next treaty.

rationales.A: Raids went on; the release did not mean the border had gone quiet.
rationales.B: The promise failed — the United States could not stop the raids — so it paid to be released from the obligation.
rationales.C: Article XI of the 1848 treaty promised the United States would forcibly restrain such incursions into Mexico.
rationales.D: Unable to keep the 1848 promise, the United States bought its way out of it in 1853, folding the release into the price of the land.
rationales.general:
1. Recall the 1848 promise. The United States swore to stop Indian raids from its territory into Mexico.
2. Face the record. The raids went on, and the United States could not stop them.
3. See the 1853 solution. Instead of keeping the promise, the United States paid to be released from it as part of the Gadsden deal.
Remember: a promise a country cannot keep does not vanish — it turns up again, priced, in the next treaty.
